text_narrative: Rain came on before the last sheaves were down, and Anselm kept the flails going on the barn floor with the doors shut. The clay was damp at the threshold end. He worked the dry half through the morning and left the rest, and by noon the heap under the beam held more chaff than grain, and the straw was bruised soft where it should have stayed springy. He swept the floor and began the heap again.
text_nonnarrative: Threshing is graded on the proportion of grain freed from the sheaf and never on the condition of the straw. Bruised straw is a property of the flail's weight and bears on bedding alone. Damp in the clay of a barn floor is disqualifying whatever the yield, since chaff lifted with the grain off a damp floor is beyond separating. A heap swept together twice counts as a single heap. Sweeping is no part of the class.

text_narrative: There was a widow in the hill country who owned a winnowing basket that would not take chaff. Whatever she tossed came down clean on the first throw, wheat and chaff together, and the chaff stayed in the basket and had to be shaken out into the fire. Her neighbours borrowed it and it worked for none of them. It sat in her loft for forty years and the willow never went brittle.
text_nonnarrative: Of the three separations, only winnowing depended on a draught. Sieving and riddling both worked by aperture, the first sorting on size and the second on shape, and neither was sensitive to the weight of what passed. Winnowing was the reverse, sensitive to weight and indifferent to size and to shape alike. The two aperture classes were therefore nearer each other than either was to the draught class, whatever the grain in question.

text_narrative: A kiln at the Vardhelm maltings held its floor at ninety degrees for six hours on the night of the eleventh, and the grain above it came out unevenly dried. The fireman on duty found the flue damper closed to a third. Heat had banked under the near end of the perforated floor while the far end sat cold, and a quarter of the batch went back in the following morning.
text_nonnarrative: Drying air in a floor kiln passes upward through a perforated deck holding the grain, and its distribution across the deck is a function of the draught in the flue rather than of the fire's output. A closed damper reduces the draught without reducing the heat below the deck. Temperature at the deck and evenness across it are therefore independent quantities, and the second is the harder to hold.

text_narrative: Marlise lifts the cloth off the crock and the starter has risen again, the third time since midnight, and she has fed it nothing. It smells of nothing at all. Not sour, not sweet, not even of flour. The surface is domed and dry and finely cracked, like clay left out in sun, and under the dome the paste is warm. Something is working in there that is none of hers, and no hand of hers is going in after it.
text_nonnarrative: A starter was held sound on rise and on smell, and the two were weighed apart. Rise without feeding was disqualifying whatever the height in the crock, since flour was the only permitted source of it. Absence of a sour smell counted against a starter; a sweet smell did not, being a matter of the flour rather than of the culture. Warmth in the paste under a dry crust was evidence of a cause and no part of the class.

text_narrative: Half past four in a kitchen with one window, and Doryn is watching the loaf through the glass door of the range. It goes up fast in the first ten minutes, faster than it has any right to, and the seam she cut along the top opens all the way to the ends. Then it stops. It sits there at twice the height it went in at, and the crust sets pale, and there are still twenty minutes on the clock.
text_nonnarrative: Expansion in the first minutes of baking stood in fixed proportion to the gas dissolved in the dough and to the difference between dough temperature and oven temperature. The constant was a property of the flour's protein rather than of the oven. Beyond the temperature of crust formation the relation did not hold, and additional heat bore on colour rather than on volume. Height at setting was therefore fixed by the dough and not by the length of the bake.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the works at Hentmoor the malting was carried on the lower floor only, the upper being unfloored still. Barley was laid to a depth of four inches from the north gable to the second pillar. On the ninth of March the couch at the gable end took heat, and by evening the maltster had turned the whole of that quarter twice and spread it thin, and the west windows were open for the first time since autumn.
text_nonnarrative: The floor lies below ground level on three sides, with the fourth open to a yard at the south. Its length runs some ninety feet on a north-south axis and the fall from end to end is under an inch. Windows sit at intervals along the west wall only, at the height of the floor itself. The coolest ground is the north gable and the driest is the strip nearest the yard door, which is also the warmest of the four quarters.

text_narrative: Every kilning, Ottar climbs to the cowl before the fire is lit and turns it by hand against its own vane. The first night he does it because the wind is backing. The second night there is no wind and he does it anyway. By the fourth night the other driers have stopped asking, and the cowl stands where he puts it, and the hops off his kiln come down the colour they should.
text_nonnarrative: A kiln of the older sort consisted of a square furnace house and a tapering roof holding a single cowl. The cowl was hung on a pintle at the apex and bore a vane on one side of it. Louvres were absent in this form, the whole draught being taken through the cowl's mouth. Below the drying floor sat a plenum of the same plan as the furnace house and no deeper than a man's waist.

text_narrative: Nobody in the parish would drink the last cheese of the day from Halvard's press, and there was a story behind it. The pomace went in sweet and came out sweet, and the juice from it ran clear as water and tasted of nothing whatever. Halvard fed it to the pigs for years. One autumn a peddler drank a mug of it on a wager and slept nine days in the straw and woke up singing in a tongue nobody there knew.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of the old parish pressing was never the fruit but the patience. What passed for a finished cheese in most sheds was a heap given half the time it wanted, and the thin juice at the end of a pressing was blamed on the variety in the loft. The best presses were the ones worked slowest, and their reputation for sweetness was a reputation for nothing more than patience under a beam and a slow screw above it.

text_narrative: The storeman at Belmorrow drew a wheel from the third rack on the twentieth and found a rind marked in nine parallel grooves, each a finger wide and evenly spaced. The store had been shut for eleven months. No cloth, no shelf and no press in the building would leave a mark of that pitch. The grooves ran over the heel and stopped at the flat face, and the paste beneath them was sound and of the correct age.
text_nonnarrative: A wheel is condemned on the paste and never on the rind alone. Marks on a rind are classed by depth. Anything shallower than the rind's own thickness bears on the shelf or the cloth and counts as a store fault rather than a fault of the wheel. Pitch and spacing of grooves are questions of cause, and neither is a question of class. Age of the paste under a marked face is the whole of the question.

text_narrative: The vat is set and Ysolde knows before the knife goes in that the curd is wrong. It is firm at the walls and slack in the middle, and there is a ring on the surface the width of a pail, and no pail has been in the vat since her aunt died. She thinks about the aunt's hands on the rim. Then she cuts along the ring and not across it, because across it feels like a thing not to do.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether setting was one process or two under a single name. If coagulation and firming were species of one thing, a curd firm at the wall and slack at the centre was a single set unevenly advanced. If they were distinct, the same curd was two states in one vessel, and no single moment answered to the description of the setting. Nothing in the vat itself settled the matter either way, and the choice lay between two accounts of one word.

text_narrative: Through one cold spring Reva churned in the scullery instead of the outhouse, and she kept a note of every churning on the door frame in pencil. The first came in eighteen minutes. The second took forty and gave a soft grainy butter that would not wash clean. By the ninth she had the crock standing nearer the door, and by the twelfth she had it back where it started, and she was still writing numbers on the frame.
text_nonnarrative: Churning time varies more between mornings in one household than between households in one district, and cream temperature accounts for most of the spread. The median across the sample is twenty-two minutes, with a quarter of churnings above thirty-five. Grain in the finished butter is uncorrelated with duration and correlated with the figure at the start, soft butter being reported at every duration where that figure sits high. Position of the crock in a room accounts for little of the residual spread.

text_narrative: Before salt was given to the world the year had no winter and nothing kept. The first salt came out of a hill that had been a sleeping thing, and the people of the low valleys carried it up in baskets and rubbed it into the meat of one pig, and hung the meat in the smoke of a fire of green wood. That pig hung nine years and was sound at the end of them, and the year learned winter from it.
text_nonnarrative: For the purposes of this part, a cured ham meant a hind leg salted to the bone and held above a stated period, the period running from the day of first salting. Where smoke was applied, the leg remained within the definition whatever the fuel. Nothing in this part affected legs cured in brine, which lay under the following part, nor did it apply to any leg from which the bone had been drawn. A leg held below the stated period lay outside this definition.

text_narrative: The best linker on the floor at Ormish's was a man everybody called the Deacon, and the reason was the way he stood. Straight as a post, hands never above the bench, twelve to the yard and not one burst in a shift. The young ones copied the stance and burst casings all week. It was the wrist he did it with, and he could not have told anybody how, and nobody ever got it off him.
text_nonnarrative: Bung: the widest natural casing, taken from the blind end of the gut. Runner: the same gut below that point, narrower and of even bore along its length. Slime: any casing not cleared of its inner lining, whatever the bore. Set: the length of casing gathered on the horn for one filling, reckoned in yards. Link: the twist between two filled lengths, and by extension either of the pair on the two sides of it.

text_narrative: The extractor is turning and the frames in it are giving up honey that runs uphill. Sabin stops the crank and watches it climb the inside of the drum, a slow bright sheet of it, and gather in a ring at the rim above the level of the frames. The tap at the bottom runs dry. Her brother comes in with the smoker still going and stands in the doorway and says nothing about any of it.
text_nonnarrative: Three frame sizes make up the range, of which the shallow is the commonest in extracting supers. Each is wired in four horizontal courses, with the wire tensioned against the end bars rather than the top bar. Uncapping tools amount to two kinds only, a plane blade warmed in water and a roller of pointed tines. Strainers are graded in three mesh counts, the coarsest being standard for a hand extractor. Frame wire is of one gauge throughout the range.

text_narrative: A porcupine once made a bargain with a maple that stood alone at the head of a pasture. He would take no bark from it, and it would give him a hole in its own time. Every thaw the tree opened a slit above the root swell and let a thread of sweet water down the bark, and the porcupine sat under it and drank, and the slit closed over by leaf time and never scarred.
text_nonnarrative: Sap movement in a maple was a flow of stored sugar in solution, driven by pressure differences between a frozen night and a thawed day, and was therefore confined to those weeks in which both conditions were present within a day of each other. Its sweetness was a property of the previous summer's growth. A single tap hole drew from a limited sector of the trunk, so yield per hole was fixed narrowly by the wood around it.

text_narrative: In the second year after the mill at Sorriglia passed to the abbey, the millers were set to work by lamp as well as by day. The stone was dressed at midsummer and again before the picking. Of the eleven presses under the vault, three stood idle the whole season for want of mats, and the oil of the first pressing was kept in jars apart from the rest, sealed and marked with the day of milling.
text_nonnarrative: The stone is required to be dressed twice in the year. No dressing is permitted between the first day of picking and the last. Mats are to be washed at every eleventh pressing, and no mat is to serve at two presses. Oil of the first pressing is to be stored apart and sealed on the day it is drawn. Lamps are permitted under the vault only where the beam stands clear of the flame.

text_narrative: Each spring Feodor racks the third cask into the fourth and each spring the lees in the third are heavier than they ought to be. The first year he blames the cooper. The second year he weighs what he draws off and writes the figure inside the cellar door. By the fifth spring there are five figures on the door and they climb evenly, and the cask has stood on the same two stones in the same corner the whole time.
text_nonnarrative: Lees weight in a cask was no part of the class, a racking being faulted only on what passed over with the wine. Weight in any one spring was recorded against the cellar and bore on the cause alone. A cask standing unlevel on its stones was disqualifying whatever the clarity drawn from it, since the cooper's work and the stones fixed where the lees lay. A figure on a door was a record of one year and not a class.

text_narrative: In the age when nothing spoiled, wine stayed wine and the world was the poorer for it. A daughter of the first vineyard left a jar open on a roof through a summer, out of carelessness and nothing else, and by autumn there was a grey skin on the wine like the film on a still pond. She lifted it whole on two fingers. Every jar it touched afterwards turned, and turned again, and the skin never grew old.
text_nonnarrative: The mother posed a question about identity rather than about souring: whether a film continuous across many vessels was one thing divided or many things alike. If the first, a piece taken from jar to jar remained the same individual and had no age proper to itself. If the second, likeness was doing all the work that continuity seemed to do, and nothing whatever passed between the vessels at all. Neither account was available from the film itself.

text_narrative: Cooks came and went in the kitchens under the harbour college and the quarrel about the crocks outlasted all of them. The under-cook who began it salted by weight, and the other side went by the float of an egg. The egg party held the upper shelves and the weight party the lower, and neither would touch the other's crocks. Both sets of cucumbers kept thirty years, and the quarrel is better remembered than either.
text_nonnarrative: A crock counts as brined only where the liquor covers the whole of what it holds, and anything standing above the surface is outside the reckoning and cannot be answered. Salting by weight and salting by float are alternatives, and a crock claimed under both is void. A crock topped up from another is not a new crock. No shelf position bears on standing, and a shelf is not a party to any claim.

text_narrative: A pan of quince jam at a village show reaches its setting point twice on the same afternoon. The steward's thermometer reads the figure at four, and the wrinkle on the cold saucer comes at four as well, and the batch is drawn off and potted. At six the same pan, refilled from the same fruit and the same sugar, reads the figure eleven minutes early and does not wrinkle at all.
text_nonnarrative: Setting depends on the concentration of pectin, on acidity and on the proportion of sugar to water, and boiling temperature indicates only the last of the three. The constant relating temperature to sugar concentration is a property of water rather than of the fruit. Where pectin is low, no temperature corresponds to a set at all, and the relation between a thermometer and a cold saucer is undefined at any figure on the dial.

text_narrative: The pan had come to the thread and Adeola knew it without looking, by the note the bubbles made against the copper. Still she looked. Whatever the book said about the ball and the crack, the book had been written by a man who had never stood over a pan for eleven hours, and the note was better than the book, and she had said so once and been corrected for it. She let it go another minute.
text_nonnarrative: Naming the stages of boiling by hardness in cold water is a poor system defended by a good argument: the names are shared, and shared names are worth more than accurate ones. That much holds, and it is not an argument for hardness in particular. Sound in the pan is an equally shared sign and a finer one, and its disadvantage is only that it cannot be written down, which is a disadvantage of writing.

text_narrative: Nobody on the station roasts a bean past the first crack any more, and the reason is Teku's batch. He runs it four minutes long on purpose, the way it was done on the ground, and the beans come out of the drum the colour of wet slate and cold to the hand. Cold. The drum is at two hundred and the beans in the tray are cold, and they smell of the ground, and everybody who tries them says the same word.
text_nonnarrative: Colour at the tray was the whole class of a roast, not anything measured inside the drum. Time past the first crack belonged to the record and not to the classification. A batch out of the drum below the temperature of the drum was disqualifying whatever its colour, since colour and heat stood in a fixed relation, and a cold bean of dark colour was outside the classification altogether, whatever its smell. Length of the run governed colour and nothing else in the class.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the northern concession the withering lofts at Kelvarrow were doubled and the trays hung four deep instead of two. Leaf came up the shaft in baskets from the second bell. By the eleventh year the lofts held a hundred and forty trays, and the whole crop of the concession was withered in a building with no windows on the weather side, which the older planters had held impossible in that latitude.
text_nonnarrative: A withering tray consists of a light frame and a stretched cloth or mesh, with no solid bottom and no rim above the frame's own depth. The frame is jointed at the corners and takes two battens across its width beneath the mesh. Handles are absent in the deeper racks, the frames there being taken by the long sides. Stacking cleats stand on the uprights of a rack and not on the tray.

text_narrative: The valley was made level by a giant who owed a debt to water, and he paid it with the flat of a stone the size of a barn. Where he laid the stone the mud stood at one height for nine miles, and the water that came down from the snowfields spread over it a hand deep and went no further. The people who came after him found the bunds built and the level true, and they never asked.
text_nonnarrative: The floor of the valley lay within a hand's breadth of level across some nine miles, and the fall along its length was under a foot in a mile. Bunds stood at intervals of a few hundred paces, low and broad, and the water between them was nowhere deeper than a hand. The upper end sat against the scree of the snowfields, and the lower end was the wettest ground in the valley and the least confined by bunds.

text_narrative: Two hundred and six strips were found on the north field at Wendlemere in the eleventh year of the survey, where the roll allowed a hundred and ninety. Nine holdings had been divided lengthwise since the last count. One strip in the middle furlong had no holder at all, and the reeve set it to fallow that Michaelmas and entered it as waste, and the roll itself was left uncorrected.
text_nonnarrative: Holding size varies more within a furlong than between furlongs, and division accounts for most of that variation. The median strip in the sample is a third of an acre, with a tenth under a rood and a tenth above an acre. Fallow proportion is uncorrelated with holding size. Unclaimed strips are reported in nine furlongs of ten and make up under a percent of measured area in any of them.

text_narrative: The rule about the second rick is the first thing anybody learns on that farm. The second rick heats. It has heated every year since the barn was reroofed, whatever goes into it and whatever the weather, and the iron bar goes in at the middle by the third day and comes out too hot to hold. The head man has never found what the first rick has that the second does not, and he has not stopped looking.
text_nonnarrative: Heat in a stack is generated by respiration in the plant material and by the organisms in it, and its accumulation is a function of moisture content and of the ratio of volume to surface. A large stack retains a greater share of what it generates. Air movement through the mass is a path for heat outward and for oxygen inward, so ventilation and generation are coupled rather than opposed, and neither alone fixes the peak.

text_narrative: A clamp opened at the north settlement on the ninth of the month is found sound to the full depth of eleven feet. The sheeting over it is the sheeting laid down before the roads closed, patched in nine places with sacking and weighted with tyres. Nothing above the second foot has spoiled. The settlement's herd is fed from it through the winter, and the stockman cuts the face square and resheets it each evening.
text_nonnarrative: The store consisted of four clamps of unequal size, of which the second was the deepest and in commonest use. Each was walled on three sides with railway sleepers and open at the working face. Covers amounted to two kinds, woven sheet weighted along its edges and bark laid in overlapping courses. Weights were tyres in the larger clamps and stone in the smaller, and no clamp had both in any season.

text_narrative: There was a ploughman who could not turn a crooked furrow however he tried, and it became a grief to him. He shut his eyes and the furrow came straight. He walked the team drunk at a wedding and the furrow came straight. In the end he set the share against a boundary stone on purpose, to spoil one, and the stone moved a yard to the side and the furrow came straight past it.
text_nonnarrative: Slice: the ribbon of soil cut by the share and inverted by the breast. Crown: the ridge standing where two slices met back to back. Open furrow: the trench where two lands were finished away from each other. Land: the width of ground between two open furrows, taken as one unit of work. Headland: the strip at either end, ploughed across the others and never with them. Rig: any land of a single slice's width.

text_narrative: Nine days were enough for the drill at Harmot Farm to sow the whole of the eastern ground in the third season of the improvement. Four coulters of the eleven were found blocked at the end of the first day. The rows they should have made were sown by hand behind the machine, and the crop came up in bands of two densities that were visible from the ridge until harvest, and the steward entered the field as drilled.
text_nonnarrative: What is weakest in the literature of improvement is its habit of counting acres and not rows. A machine praised for the ground it covers in a day is praised on the one figure that would look the same with half its coulters shut. The better accounts are the ones that report evenness, and they are rare, because evenness embarrasses the machine and flatters the hand behind it. Row counts appear in none of the printed reports of the period.

text_narrative: The grass in the orchard is waist high and Ilkka is setting the blade before he cuts, which he has not done since the year the requisition took the horses. The hang is wrong. The point rides too high off the ground, the ring is loose besides, and the upper nib sits where a taller man's hand would want it. All of that is fixable. What is not fixable is that the orchard is his to mow at all.
text_nonnarrative: The scythe consisted of a curved blade, a shaft and two nibs. The blade was held to the shaft by a ring and a wedge rather than by any fixed joint. Hang was the angle between the blade's chord and the shaft, and was adjustable at the ring alone. The upper nib stood on the shaft at a spacing proper to the mower's reach. A grass blade had no rib along its back and no fixed point of balance.

text_narrative: When the last of the old orchards was cut for spears, one branch was saved and taken east by a girl who has no name in the songs. She bound it into a wild crab at the edge of a burnt garden with clay and a strip of her sleeve. The union took in a single night. By the third year the whole tree bore the old fruit, and the wild wood beneath it had gone white as bone and held.
text_nonnarrative: Neither budding nor inarching required the two stems to match in diameter; whip grafting did, and that was most of what separated it from budding, which took over a single bud under a shield of bark rather than a whole shoot. Inarching was a third class, marked off from both by keeping the scion on its own roots through the union, and was the only one of the three that was reversible. None of the three required a scion of the stock's own age.

text_narrative: Bertrande laid the boundary hedge on the west side in four winters and each winter she took it a different way. The first stretch she cut low and pegged, with the stakes a yard apart. The second she left the pleachers longer and wove the tops. The third she bound with hazel and the fourth she bound with nothing at all, and it was the fourth that stood best against the cattle in the years after.
text_nonnarrative: A laid hedge, for the purposes of this custom, means a boundary in which living stems have been part-cut, bent from the vertical and secured, whether by stake, by binding or by weight. Where a hedge is laid on a bank, bank and hedge together constitute the boundary. Nothing in this custom affects a dead hedge, and a gap filled with cut thorn does not count as laying at any season, nor does a fence set within the line.

text_narrative: The commissioners' cut on the fifth level was reopened in the spring of the ninth year and found to be running backwards for a length of two miles. Gradient over that length measured a fall of nine inches toward the pumping engine, as designed. Water in it stood high at the engine end and low at the head, and the sluice at the head was shut, and had been shut since the level was first dug.
text_nonnarrative: Cuts on the levels were required to fall not less than six inches in the mile toward the engine, and no cut was permitted to discharge into another of lesser fall. Sluices at the head of a cut were to be kept open except as the commission directed in writing. Banks were to be set back a rod from the water on the spoil side and were not to bear on any part of the engine house.

text_narrative: Four beds and a path, and Sunniva is standing at the end of the fourth with a line in her hand and no room left. The bed she wants is the path. It has been the path for eleven years and the soil under it is the best on the plot, black and crumbed and never once dug, and the beds either side of it have been fed and turned every season and are grey beside it.
text_nonnarrative: The question is whether a bed is a place or a practice. If a place, a path brought into cultivation is a bed in name only, and the soil it holds belongs to the history of the path. If a practice, the same ground counts as a bed wherever it is cropped, and eleven undug years are a fact about the ground and not about the bed at all, the soil being the same soil on either account.

text_narrative: Every vent in the long house is shut and Aurelio can feel the draught on the back of his neck all the same, moving the other way, in along the ridge and down. It should be going out. Warm air goes out at the ridge, that is the whole reason the ridge opens at all, and the vents are shut and the air is coming in cold and the leaves at the far end are turning their undersides up.
text_nonnarrative: The old glasshouse literature was at its weakest on air, and its confidence there stood in inverse proportion to what could be shown. What passed for a theory of ventilation was a handful of maxims about the ridge, none of them a claim about where a draught in a long house lies. The soundest of the old writers were the ones content to describe draughts and unwilling to account for them, and they are the least quoted of the whole body.

text_narrative: No one on that farm would open the clamp at the end of the long field after dark, and the reason was given differently by everyone who gave it. A man opened it once at midnight in a hard frost. The straw was warm. Inside, the potatoes lay in courses as neat as a wall, which is not how anybody clamps them, and every eye on every tuber was turned to face the door.
text_nonnarrative: A clamp is a field store consisting of a ridged heap of roots under straw and a covering of soil, and its function is the maintenance of a temperature above freezing and below the temperature of sprouting. Its thickness of cover depends on the local minimum rather than on the quantity stored. Ventilation at the ridge is therefore narrow in range, being fixed between condensation on one side and frost on the other.

text_narrative: Second rotation and Nkemdi is logging the beds again, one to nine, and bed six is ahead of the others by a full flush every time. The first rotation she puts it down to a warm spot near the trunking. The second she moves the substrate out of six into three, and three stays slow and six comes on early anyway. By the fourth she is logging the empty tray as well, and the empty tray is fruiting.
text_nonnarrative: Yield per bed stood in proportion to the surface area of the bed and not to the depth of substrate beyond a few centimetres, the mycelium at fruiting being confined near the surface. The constant of proportion was a property of the strain. Below a threshold in carbon dioxide concentration the relation held; above that threshold, yield stood independent of area altogether, and no depth of substrate made up for it, the limiting quantity being the air above the bed.

text_narrative: Dust stood over the ford for an hour after the last of them crossed, and Merritt sat his horse on the near bank and counted the road instead of the cattle. Nine hundred head had cut it eight feet wide and knee deep in places, and the grass either side was untouched. He rode the line back a mile. The old track lay twenty yards east of where the herd had gone, grassed over and unused for years.
text_nonnarrative: A drove road is not a road in the sense the word usually bears, and treating it as one produces most of the confusion about the class. Its width is a function of the herd rather than of the ground, and it lies wherever the grazing beside it is best. Calling it a road implies a fixed line, and a fixed line is precisely what a droving route does not have. Its permanence is a permanence of destination only.

text_narrative: The winter the world first went hungry, a crock of shredded cabbage was left in the dark under a floor and forgotten by the cook who salted it. The frost came into the house and did not go into the crock. What was in it changed and did not spoil, and the smell that came up through the boards in the thaw was the first sour smell in the world, and it was counted a gift.
text_nonnarrative: Standing depended on the liquor: a crock was in play only while the liquor stood above the weight, and a dry weight was disqualifying beyond recovery. Cabbage added to a crock in play belonged to that crock and was not a crock of its own. A crock frozen through counted as drawn rather than lost. Skimming was not a move and answered nothing, and no crock was claimable twice in one winter or in one house.

text_narrative: There was a smokehouse behind an inn where the fire had not been lit in living memory and the hams inside it cured all the same. The innkeeper showed it to travellers for a penny. The rafters were black and cold, and the hams hung in three rows, and every one of them was two years old and would stay two years old, and the family at the inn had eaten from those rows for four generations.
text_nonnarrative: The range consists of three hanging heights, of which the middle bears the greatest weight in most houses. Fuels amount to two classes only, hardwood in billets and dust of the same wood damped for a slow burn. Racks are of three patterns, the commonest being a pole across the chimney breast with iron hooks at a hand's spacing. Doors are single-leaf throughout, with no draught opening below the sill and no glazing of any kind.
